newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba will have to back down in gold row - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Buba will have to back down in gold row - analyst.

text.p: The Bundesbank will have to back down in its confrontation with the Bonn government over the revaluation of gold reserves although it may be able to secure some "cosmetic" concessions," senior economist with Commerzbank AG said on Friday.

Juergen Pfister told Reuters in an interview that Finance Minister Theo Waigel could not afford to scrap his plan to require the Bundesbank to pay out a special profit this year from the revaluation of the bank's gold and currency reserves.

While the move was a setback to hopes that the planned European Central Bank would be completely independent, it need not mean the single currency, or euro, would be soft, or that monetary union would start with a larger number of members than previously envisaged, Pfister said.
"The Bundesbank will have to back down because this question is in the domain of the government," Pfister said.

"I could imagine there will be some compromise on the extent and method of the payout. But I don't think Waigel will back down because he will want to avoid losing face and will want to make sure Germany meets the Maastricht criteria."
Pfister said the Bundesbank may persuade Bonn to put a part of the valuation gain in a special revaluation reserve rather than using it to retire public debt.
But this would only be "cosmetic" because it would not affect the main issue of forcing the Bundesbank to transfer money to Bonn in 1997.

Bonn is believed to be seeking a transfer of 20 billion marks in total from the revaluation, well below the 40 billion marks in existing hidden reserves of gold -- the difference between the market price and the value at which it is currently booked in Bundesbank accounts.
But Pfister said Waigel's plan, criticised by the Bundesbank in a sharply-worded statement on Wednesday, "demonstrates what independence means in the case of conflict."
Waigel's plan is aimed at plugging gaping holes in Germany's finances to enable the country to qualify for monetary union.
The proposal has been widely criticised as the same sort of accounting trickery that Germany has accused other European Union nations of in the drive to meet the convergence criteria.

Pfister said Bonn wanted to meet the Maastricht convergence criteria to the letter because this would give it a greater say in choosing which nations can form the starting line-up for monetary union, scheduled to begin on January 1, 1999.
"We are all tricksters now," Pfister said, adding that some tricksters would manage to meet the criteria while others would not. "Vive la difference."

Given pending legislation on the required amendments to the Bundesbank law, Bonn and the central bank were likely to come to some sort of agreement in the coming weeks, Pfister said. The revaluation plan will go before parliament in early June.
The Bundesbank on Wednesday slammed Waigel's plan as an interference with its independence, which ran the risk of damaging the credibility of the planned single currency.
The revaluation of the Bundesbank's reserves is necessary in any case as part of preparations for the transfer of reserves to the European Central Bank.
But Waigel wants to bring the revaluation forward to 1997 and to require the Bundesbank to pay out part of the valuation in tranches, one in 1997.
Under Bonn's plans the money would flow into the Inherited Debt Redemption Fund and thereby reduce the public debt.
Pfister said that transfer would also help reduce the budget deficit because it would mean the Redemption Fund had more money than it needed to service its debts this year.
The resulting surplus would be booked in the government's budget, Pfister said.
--David Crossland, Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
